l: male goat (vision of the goat), Daniel (Greek)
s: A vision symbol: the male goat, which Gabriel interprets as the king of Greece. It arrives from the west over the whole earth without touching the ground, furiously attacks the ram, and grows proud. At its strength its great horn, the first king, breaks, and four lesser horns, four kingdoms, replace it.

l: little horn (arising from the goat's horns), Daniel (Greek)
s: The little horn arises from one of the goat's four notable horns and grows exceedingly great toward the south, east, and glorious land. It casts down part of the army and stars, magnifies itself against the prince of the army, takes away the continual burnt offering, throws down the sanctuary, and casts truth to the ground. Gabriel interprets it as a fierce-faced king whose mighty power is not his own, who destroys the holy people by deceit, and who, after standing against the prince of princes, is broken without human power.

Gabriel is a man-like being who serves as interpreter and giver of wisdom and understanding to Daniel. In Chapter 8, a voice between the banks of the Ulai commands him to explain the vision; he touches and steadies the fallen Daniel, explains the ram, goat, horns and fierce-faced king, and says the vision is true but sealed. In Chapter 9, he flies swiftly at the evening offering, instructs Daniel, and delivers the seventy weeks message.

The vision of the evenings and mornings, shown in Chapter 8, depicts a ram, a goat, a great horn broken into four, and a little horn desecrating the sanctuary for 2,300 evenings and mornings until cleansing. Gabriel declares it true, belonging to the time of the end, and tells Daniel to seal it, though no one understands.

Daniel's prayer, addressed to God with fasting in sackcloth and ashes, confesses Israel's sin, rebellion and ignored prophets, affirms God's righteousness, then pleads for forgiveness and prompt action on Jerusalem, resting on God's mercies, not merit.

is_a period [word of the LORD to Jeremiah for the desolations of Jerusalem] Daniel understands from the books that the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet set seventy years for accomplishing the desolations of Jerusalem. This realization prompts him to seek God in prayer and fasting.

The seventy weeks prophecy, delivered by Gabriel in Chapter 9, is a decree upon Daniel's people and holy city. Its purposes are to end sin, reconcile iniquity, bring everlasting righteousness, seal up vision and prophecy, and anoint the most holy. It unfolds from the commandment to restore Jerusalem through seven and sixty-two weeks to the Anointed One, then a final week of covenant, ceased sacrifice, and wrath on the desolate.
A prince called the Anointed One, foretold in Chapter 9 to come after seven and sixty-two weeks from the order to rebuild Jerusalem, who makes a firm covenant with many, then is cut off with nothing.

Israel's sin is rebellion against God's law: all Israel transgressed, ignored the prophets, and did not turn from iniquity. It brought the written curse and great evil on Jerusalem, and Daniel acknowledges God's righteousness in sending it.

A radiant being clothed in linen, with gold-adorned thighs, a beryl body, lightning face, flaming-torch eyes, bronze arms and feet, and a multitude-like voice. In Chapter 10 he is sent to Daniel because Daniel's words were heard, explains he was withstood twenty-one days by the prince of Persia until Michael helped, and comes to reveal what will befall Daniel's people in the latter days. He strengthens Daniel and says he will return to fight the prince of Persia, after which the prince of Greece will come. In Chapter 12, above the river's waters, he raises both hands and swears by him who lives forever that the end will come in a time, times, and a half.

Michael is a chief and great prince, the protector of Daniel's people. In Chapter 10 he helps the speaker after the prince of Persia withstands him for twenty-one days, and alone supports him against the princes of Persia and Greece. In Chapter 12 he stands up at the time of trouble, and the people are delivered.

rules Persia [prince of the kingdom] The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood the man clothed in linen for twenty-one days, until Michael came to help. The man says he will return to fight this prince, and that the prince of Greece will come when he goes out.
has_fate delivered [everyone found written in the book] Daniel's people are said to be delivered at the time of trouble, everyone who is found written in the book. Michael stands for them.

A true revelation of a great warfare, given to Daniel in Cyrus's third year. Daniel understands the vision. The man clothed in linen explains it shows what will befall his people in the latter days, pointing to many days ahead.

Daniel's three-week mourning is a fast from pleasant bread, meat, wine and anointing, lasting until fulfilled; the linen-clad man later says his words were heard from the first day he humbled himself.

has_power_over Egypt [its treasures of gold, silver and precious things] The king of the north is repeatedly in conflict with the king of the south, being attacked by the southern king's successor, who carries off gods and treasures to Egypt, then returning with greater armies, taking a well-fortified city and standing in the glorious land. He gives the daughter of women to corrupt, but she does not stand for him. At the time of the end he comes like a whirlwind with chariots, horsemen and ships, overflows the countries and Egypt, is troubled by news from the east and north, and pitches his palace tents between the sea and the glorious holy mountain before coming to his end with no one to help him.

has_attribute strong The king of the south is strong, and one of his princes becomes stronger and rules a great dominion. His daughter goes to the king of the north to make an agreement but fails to keep her strength. He is moved with anger and fights the northern king, gaining a multitude but not prevailing, and later loses a war against a great army because those who ate his delicacies devise plans against him. At the time of the end he contends with the self-exalting king.

A contemptible person rises to a kingdom's throne without being granted its honor. He arrives in a time of security, gains power through flatteries, sweeps away forces and the prince of the covenant, and grows strong through deceit after a treaty. He plunders, attacks strongholds and the king of the south, then, opposed by Kittim's ships, turns hostile against the holy covenant.

The holy covenant becomes the object of hostility when the king returns to his land with great wealth and his heart is against it. He has indignation against it, takes action, and favors those who forsake it. His forces profane the sanctuary, remove the continual burnt offering, and set up the abomination that makes desolate, while he corrupts covenant-breakers by flatteries.

has_role instruct many [yet they will fall by sword, flame, captivity and plunder] The wise among the people instruct many, yet fall by sword, flame, captivity and plunder for many days. When they fall they receive a little help, while many join them with flatteries. Some of the wise fall to refine, purify and make them white until the time of the end, which is still for the appointed time.

A self-exalting king acts by his own will, magnifies himself above every god, and speaks marvelous things against the God of gods. He prospers until the indignation is accomplished, ignores his fathers' gods, and honors an unknown god of fortresses with treasures. With that foreign god's help he conquers fortresses, elevates his supporters, and divides the land for a price.

has_attribute increased knowledge [many run back and forth] The time of the end is the point until which Daniel's words remain sealed. It is marked by increased knowledge, the purifying of many, the wicked doing wickedly, and the 1,290 and 1,335 day periods from the removal of the continual burnt offering and the setting up of the abomination that makes desolate.

l: those who sleep in the dust of the earth, Daniel (Greek)
s: has_fate awake [many of them; some to everlasting life, some to shame and everlasting contempt] Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake. Some will awake to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
The wise are a group who understand what the wicked cannot; in the time of the end, their fate is to shine like the expanse's brightness, like stars forever.

has_attribute unprecedented [such as never was since there was a nation] The time of trouble is described as one such as never was since there was a nation. It occurs when Michael stands up, and the people are delivered during it.

remains_sealed_until time of the end Daniel is commanded to shut up the words and seal the book until the time of the end. He is told again that the words are shut up and sealed until then, though many will run back and forth and knowledge will increase.

Susanna, daughter of Helkias and wife of Joakim, is a fair, delicate, devout woman from Judah, taught the law of Moses by her parents. Threatened by two elders in the garden, she refuses to sin and cries out. Falsely accused and condemned to death, she prays to God and is saved when Daniel exposes the lie.

Joakim is a very wealthy, highly honored Babylonian husband of Susanna, owning a garden beside his house where Jews and elder-judges visit; after Susanna is vindicated, he joins her kin in praising God.

Two elders, appointed judges that year, frequent Joakim's house where litigants come. Lustful toward Susanna, they spy on her, ambush her in the garden, and falsely accuse her when refused. Daniel questions them separately, exposes contradictory testimony, and they are executed under the law of Moses.

has_trait beautiful The garden is the beautiful one next to Joakim's house, where Susanna walks at noon after the people depart. The two elders hide there and, once her maids have shut the doors and gone, confront her. It is the site of the alleged adultery, with the elders claiming to have seen it under a tree.

believes two elders [initially trusted them as elders and judges] The people assemble at Joakim's house and believe the elders' testimony, condemning Susanna to death. When Daniel challenges them, they return in haste to the place of judgment. After the elders' lie is exposed, they cry out, bless God who saves those who hope in him, and put the elders to death.

The young man is an invented figure whom the two elders claim they saw lying with Susanna in the garden. They say he was stronger than they, opened the doors, and leaped out, and that Susanna would not name him. Daniel's examination shows that the story, and so the young man, was a lie.

has_outcome elders executed [per the law of Moses, Susanna acquitted] The trial takes place before the assembled people at Joakim's house, where the elders have Susanna unveiled, lay hands on her head, and testify against her. The assembly believes them as elders and judges and condemns her to death. Daniel reopens the case, exposes the false testimony through separate questioning, and the sentence falls on the elders instead.

Bel is a Babylonian idol of clay and brass, worshiped daily by King Cyrus with large offerings of flour, sheep, and wine. Daniel proves it never eats or drinks, and the king gives it to him; he overthrows it and its temple.

Seventy priests of Bel, with wives and children, nightly enter a hidden entrance under Bel's table to eat the offerings. Ashes scattered by Daniel's servants reveal their footprints, and the king, shown the secret doors, kills them.
A great dragon worshiped by Babylonians and presented by the king as a living god because it eats and drinks; Daniel feeds it pitch, fat, and hair, and it bursts apart.

The people of Babylon worship the dragon and, enraged by the destruction of Bel, the dragon, and the priests, accuse the king of having become a Jew. They threaten to destroy the king and his house unless he delivers Daniel to them, and he does.
Habakkuk, a prophet in Jewry, prepares stew and bread for reapers, is carried by an angel by the hair to Babylon's den, calls Daniel to eat God's dinner, then returns instantly home.

The angel of the Lord tells Habakkuk to carry his dinner to Daniel in the lions' den in Babylon. He lifts Habakkuk by the hair of his head and sets him over the den with the blast of his breath, then returns him to his own place immediately.
A den in Babylon holding seven lions, normally fed daily but starved to devour Daniel; he survives six days unharmed, is found alive on the seventh, and his accusers are then devoured instantly.
